extracted.intended_audience: legislators, political thinkers, and readers of political philosophy (late-18th-century constitutional critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive critique and standards for designing constitutions and for the temperament and methods of legislators, arguing what makes sound representative institutions and wise lawgivers. Emphasizes practical experience, moral consideration, and social realities over abstract geometrical/arithmetic schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed slowly; use time as assistant
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of political reform ought to be slow; time is among the assistants and its operation should be gradual, in some cases almost imperceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow, cautious progress lets each step be watched; the success or failure of early steps informs later ones, preventing widespread misery from sudden alterations of sentient beings. "Our patience will achieve more than our force."

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator temperament: sensibility and humility
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lawgiver ought to have a heart full of sensibility: to love and respect his kind, and to fear himself; not an unfeeling heart with undoubting confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should be deliberate, not rash or proud; personal humility and concern for humanity are qualifications for wise legislation rather than mere confidence or boldness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social means for political arrangement (deliberation and consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political arrangement is a work for social ends and must be wrought by social means: minds must conspire with mind to produce the union necessary for good laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time is required to produce the union of minds; patient deliberation and shared reflection achieve more than unilateral force or haste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to experience and cooperative amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans should be mended by the observations of others and by experience; no plan has not been improved by contributions from those inferior in understanding to the leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test effects step by step; compensate and reconcile parts of a system as latent evils appear. Experience teaches corrections that pure theory cannot foresee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix a presiding (ruling) principle and let it operate
rubrics_metrics.description: Best legislators often establish some sure, solid, and ruling principle in government—a 'presiding principle'—and, having fixed it, leave it afterwards to its own operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed with a guiding principle and prolific energy; this approach is presented as 'the criterion of profound wisdom' contrasted with frantic overhauls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid violent haste and fashionable radicalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent haste and defiance of the processes of Nature are faults in lawgivers; such haste delivers a state to projectors, adventurers, alchemists, and empirics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick, sweeping changes favor charlatans and destroy prudential checks; patience and circumspection are moral duties when altering institutions affecting sentient beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not derive practical legislation from rhetorical paradox or satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative opinions should not be taken from declamations and buffooneries of satirists or from paradoxes produced as literary sport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradoxes used to rouse attention in literature become dangerous when treated as serious grounds of public action; imitate neither rhetorical extremes nor 'servile imitators' of fashionable thinkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary demonstration of ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who undertake to regenerate constitutions, especially when appealing to no practice or model, must display uncommon powers or very unusual appearances of wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a plan appeals to novelty rather than practice, it should evidence extraordinary competence; otherwise the claim to superior ability over mankind is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge constitutions by their effects and experiential corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Old establishments are to be tried by their effects (happiness, unity, wealth, power), and practical correctives discovered over time may make mean means serve ends better than abstract schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The means taught by experience may be better suited to political ends than those contrived in theory; theoretical perfection does not guarantee practical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely geometrical or arithmetical bases for representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation should not be founded solely on geometrical (territory) or arithmetical (population/contribution) measures without regard to political principle and human realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical division (e.g., square departments, cantons) overlooks local inconveniences and the social relations that give institutions meaning; mensuration is a ridiculous standard of political power when taken alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not impose qualifications that contradict natural equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Voting qualifications (e.g., small property or tax payments) introduced on metaphysical premises violate the principle of natural equality and establish a tyrannous aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even seemingly small qualifications (three days' labor, ten days' labor, payment of a mark of silver) undermine the declared rights of men and exclude the poorest—the very people whose equality needs protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive multi-tier indirect representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Layered representation (primary assemblies -> communes -> departments -> national assembly) erects multiple barriers between elector and representative, reducing political communion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each intermediary (qualifications, electoral colleges) taxes rights and distances the representative from constituents; such gradation undermines the immediacy of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by contribution (wealth) must target individuals/classes, not only districts
rubrics_metrics.description: Using contribution as a basis for representation that privileges districts (masses) rather than the rich individuals or a class of the rich is inconsistent and does not secure the interests of the wealthy as intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contribution is to give additional political weight, it should attach to individuals or coherent classes, not produce unequal district-based advantages that fail to benefit the supposed beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware perverse effects of unequal mass representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving a district extra representatives because it contributes more can perversely intensify the rich man's disadvantage by multiplying democratic seats and incentives for demagogues to flatter poorer voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical increases in representation can create salaries and influence for ambitious lower-status candidates, worsening the rich's prospects rather than protecting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect (consumption-based) contribution as a better indicator of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect contribution (duties on consumption) follows and discovers wealth more naturally than direct contribution assessed on presumed local wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumption duties reflect wealth distribution across regions better than direct taxes that can misattribute wealth to locales based on non-local consumers or spenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make constitution dependent on a variable taxation system
rubrics_metrics.description: If representation and qualifications are tied to direct contribution but the method of assessing contribution is unsettled, the constitution becomes variable and contingent on taxation changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions that depend on tax assessment methods invite perpetual uncertainty and internal controversies when contested elections occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure internal consistency among principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution must reconcile its various founding principles; holding contradictory principles (territory, population, contribution) together without coherence produces absurd inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing aristocratic and democratic bases without resolving tensions makes the system like 'wild beasts shut up in a cage'—prone to mutual destruction rather than productive combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study human nature, habits, and the diversity of citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators should study the effects of education, profession, residence, property, and other circumstances that produce a 'second nature' and create diversities among citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient legislators classified citizens and assigned roles and privileges suited to their capacities; modern attempts to reduce all to a homogeneous mass ignore practical differences essential to a durable republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve local knowledge, habituation, and civil connexions in office assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative and ecclesiastical offices should remain acquainted with local districts, dioceses, parishes; destroying these connections makes magistrates and collectors strangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing local habituations and discipline undermines the soul of a true republic and recreates 'colonies' of rights without the local civic character necessary for governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat a country as conquered by destroying ancient institutions wholesale
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that erase all vestiges of the ancient country—religion, polity, laws, manners—as conquerors do produce poverty, social dislocation, and the loss of means to rally people in distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruthless leveling and demolition of traditional structures risk reproducing the miseries of conquest and weaken national coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution-making must include moral and political considerations, not only abstract theory
rubrics_metrics.description: In designing constitutions, reference must be made to moral and political concerns—'the concerns, the actions, the passions, the interests of men'—not only metaphysics, geometry, and arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract scholastic principles are insufficient; a constitution must address real human motivations and social practices ('Hominem non sapiunt'—they do not understand man).
